P2100.d: P2100 reports an electrical fault in the drive circuit of the first electronic throttle motor, usually an open line. Ford's 2012 summary uses it for an open circuit or a short to power or ground (no MIL, wrench lamp).
s: Throttle held in limp position, very low power
Engine or ETC warning lamp on
Little or no response to the accelerator pedal
c: Moisture or corrosion in the throttle body or ECU connector
Broken or chafed motor wire between ECU and throttle body
Open winding or worn brushes in the throttle motor
Damaged H-bridge output stage in the engine control unit

P2101.d: Here the controller compares where throttle A should be with where its position sensors say it is. GM's 2018 table 18OBDG03A flags a gap of more than 10 percent between measured and modelled position after 15 counts at 12.5 ms each, classed by GM as Type A with immediate MIL; the 2006/2007 tables used 8.4 percent.
s: Reduced engine power message or limp mode
c: Carbon or ice makes the throttle plate stiff or sticky
High resistance at the throttle connector pins
Worn gear train or weak motor inside the throttle body
Deformed inlet duct or leak at the throttle body

P2102.d: P2102 means the output stage for throttle motor A sees a voltage or current that points to a short toward ground or an overloaded driver. GM lists P2100-P2103 together in its 2018 calibration as faults that limit engine power and default the throttle authority; a Bosch-based GM ECM of 2012 assigns its output-stage checks (short circuit, overtemperature or overcurrent, open load) to this group with about 0.1 s detecti
s: Limp mode with throttle at fixed opening
c: Motor wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Shorted winding or jammed motor drawing excess current
Water in the throttle connector bridging terminals
Faulty throttle driver in the engine control unit

P2103.d: P2103 is the high-side fault of the throttle A drive: the output stage sees a voltage that suggests a short to battery, or on some layouts the supply relay of the throttle motor stays energized when it should be off. GM groups P2100-P2103 as power-limiting faults (18OBDG03A), and its Bosch-based 2012 ECM ties a power-stage short circuit to this range with about 0.1 s detection.
s: Limp mode with very limited power
Engine may not start or stalls
c: Motor wire shorted to a battery-voltage feed
Throttle motor relay sticking on (where fitted)
Internal fault in the ECU throttle driver

P2104.d: P2104 is a status code: it does not name a broken part but records that the throttle control has switched into a forced-idle failure mode. In Ford's 2012 summary this happens on second-generation ETC systems when two or three accelerator pedal sensor tracks are lost, so the computer can no longer read driver demand; the engine then holds a raised idle and ignores the pedal, with MIL and wrench lamp.
s: Engine stays at raised idle, pedal has no effect
Engine and ETC/wrench warning lamps on
Car can only creep to a safe place
c: Failure of two or more accelerator pedal sensor tracks
Pedal sensor wiring or shared 5 V reference fault

P2105.d: P2105 is the most severe throttle failure mode: the controller has decided that throttle control can no longer be trusted and stops the engine. In Ford's 2012 summary the trigger is a serious processor fault found by the separate monitoring processor (Ford calls it the Quizzer); all injectors are switched off and the wrench lamp comes on.
s: Engine shuts off or will not keep running
Wrench or ETC warning lamp, often without MIL
c: Monitoring processor detects an internal ECU fault
Unstable ECU supply or ground connection
ECU software fault cured by reprogramming

P2106.d: P2106 tells you the throttle control is running in a reduced-power fallback. Ford's 2012 summary lists the reasons on second-generation ETC: loss of the MAF signal, one throttle position sensor, crank position or transmission speed sensors, a stuck throttle or a throttle motor circuit fault; it sets with MIL and wrench lamp, and a crank sensor code (P0320/P0322) also adds P2106.
c: Failed input such as MAF, throttle position or crank sensor
Sticking throttle or fault in the throttle motor circuit
Failed internal check or software in the engine computer

P2107.d: P2107 concerns the processor that runs throttle A control, which in most cars sits inside the engine computer rather than in a separate box. Ford's summaries define it as an internal processor fault or lost communication with the main CPU, detected within 60 ms, with MIL after two drive cycles and the ETC lamp at once; from 2024 Ford reports the same check as P2108 with a failure-type byte.
s: Engine and ETC warning lamps on
c: ECU software fault fixed by a reflash
Voltage dips or poor ECU ground
Internal hardware failure of the engine computer

P2108.d: P2108 marks a performance problem of the control function for throttle A, as opposed to a pure processor fault (P2107). VW's 2014 Touareg data book gives a concrete case: the time for the throttle to close below a reference point of 11.56 percent must not exceed 0.60 s.
s: Unstable idle after lifting off the pedal
c: Throttle closes too slowly (deposits, weak spring)
ECU software issue needing an update
Supply voltage or ground problem at the ECU

P2109.d: P2109 flags an implausible rest reading on position signal A: with the throttle or pedal resting on its lower mechanical stop, the minimum learned at key-on falls outside the window the calibration accepts. Ford names its first throttle body sensor TP A, so on such layouts the code concerns the throttle.
s: Engine warning lamp, often after a cold or wet night
Reduced power until the fault clears
c: Ice or carbon holding the throttle plate off its rest stop
ECM software with oversensitive detection (update available)
Rest position not relearned after cleaning or replacing the throttle body
Sensor A worn or drifted at the closed end of its track

P210A.d: Throttle actuator B only exists on engines with two electronic throttles, typically one per cylinder bank. P210A reports an electrical fault, mainly an open line, in the drive of that second motor.
s: Reduced power, one bank breathing poorly
c: Moisture or corrosion in the throttle B or ECU connector
Broken motor wire to throttle body B
Open winding in throttle motor B
Faulty bank 2 output stage in the ECU

P210B.d: P210B is the position-control check for the second throttle on twin-throttle engines. The controller compares the commanded opening of throttle B with the measured one; GM's 23OBDG07 table flags a deviation beyond a rate-dependent limit for 0.5 s, one trip.
s: Engine warning lamp and reduced power
Uneven running between the two banks
c: High resistance at throttle B connector pins
Deposits or ice making throttle B sluggish
Motor leads swapped after repair work
Worn gears or motor in throttle body B

P210C.d: P210C is reserved for a low-side fault in the drive circuit of the second throttle motor, for example a grounded motor lead or an overloaded output stage. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
c: Throttle B motor wire shorted to ground
Shorted or jammed throttle motor B
Faulty bank 2 throttle driver in the ECU

P210D.d: P210D covers the high-side fault of the second throttle drive: a voltage on the motor B circuit that suggests a short to battery, or a supply that stays live when the stage should be off. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
c: Throttle B motor wire shorted to battery voltage
Damaged or wet connector at throttle body B
Faulty bank 2 output stage in the ECU

P210E.d: P210E compares two redundant position signals, C and F, and sets when their voltages stop agreeing within the permitted tolerance. Which physical tracks carry these letters is up to the manufacturer: GM's 2023 table 23OBDG07 uses C for the first sensor of a second throttle body, while Ford's summaries assign D, E and F to the three tracks of its pedal, so a C/F pair only arises on unusual layouts.
s: Engine or throttle warning lamp on
Hesitant or delayed response to the pedal
c: One sensor track worn or drifted, so the pair no longer agrees
Corrosion or water in the connector shifting one signal
Fault in a shared ground or 5 V reference line
Faulty input stage in the engine control module

P210F.d: P210F is a status code for the second throttle: the controller has capped engine speed because control of throttle B is no longer reliable. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
s: Engine will not rev past a fixed limit
c: Electrical or mechanical fault of throttle B (see companion code)
Loss of the position signals of throttle B

P2110.d: P2110 records that engine speed has been capped because throttle A can no longer be controlled safely. Ford's 2012 summary sets it on second-generation ETC when both throttle position sensors fail or Ford's throttle plate controller (TPPC) reports a fault, with MIL and wrench lamp; rpm is then capped by a pedal-dependent limit enforced through fuel and spark.
s: Engine will not rev beyond a low limit
Stop/start disabled or hard start in frost
c: Ice on the throttle plate after a cold soak
Loss of both throttle position sensor signals
PCM software setting the code falsely (update available)
Worn or faulty electronic throttle body

P2111.d: P2111 means throttle A stays more open than commanded. Ford defines it precisely: the actual throttle angle exceeds the desired angle by more than 6 degrees for about 500 ms, with MIL after two drive cycles and the ETC lamp at once; it also catches a throttle that cannot bring cold-start idle down.
s: High idle speed or engine hard to slow down
Loss of power in freezing weather
c: Water or ice in the intake behind the throttle
Carbon build-up holding the plate open
Broken return spring or worn gear in the throttle body

P2112.d: P2112 is the mirror image of P2111: throttle A opens less than commanded. Ford sets it when the actual angle stays more than 6 degrees below the desired angle for about 500 ms (MIL after two drive cycles, ETC lamp at once) and lists it in its 2020-2023 and 2024 summaries.
s: Lack of power after a cold start
Low or unstable idle, possible stalling
c: Frozen condensate locking the throttle plate
Jammed gear or weak motor in the throttle body

P2113.d: The engine computer checks whether position signal B reports a plausible value when the throttle or pedal rests against its lower mechanical stop. At key-on many systems learn this minimum and compare it with a tolerance window; a reading outside that window sets the code.
s: Engine or ETC warning lamp on
c: Carbon deposits or ice keep the throttle plate off its rest stop
Position sensor B worn or drifted at the low end of its track
Minimum position not relearned after cleaning or part replacement
Corroded connector shifting the sensor B signal

P2114.d: This code reports that position signal C does not show a believable value while its throttle or pedal sits on the lower stop. The controller learns or expects a minimum reading within a tolerance band and flags a fault when the learned value falls outside it.
s: Engine or ETC warning lamp on
c: Position sensor C worn or drifted near its rest position
Deposits, ice or a damaged stop prevent the rest position
Rest position not relearned after repair
Connector or wiring fault shifting the C signal

P2115.d: Here the controller judges position signal D at the released (minimum) end of travel. On Ford and GM drive-by-wire systems D is the first accelerator pedal sensor, so the code means the pedal's idle reading is outside the expected window, for example because the pedal does not return fully or its sensor track has shifted.
s: Engine does not drop to normal idle when the pedal is released
c: Pedal blocked by floor mat or weak return spring
Worn pedal sensor track D at the idle end
Aftermarket pedal tuning module or wrong pedal part

P2116.d: The code covers the rest-position check of signal E. Ford, GM and Mitsubishi assign E to the second accelerator pedal sensor, which on many pedals runs at roughly half the voltage of sensor D (GM: APP 2 between 0.16 and 2.3 V).
c: Pedal held off its stop by floor mat or sticking pivot
Worn or contaminated sensor track E
Moisture or corrosion at the pedal connector

P2117.d: P2117 is the minimum-stop check for signal F. Ford lists F as the third accelerator pedal sensor on its older Gen2 throttle systems (circuit codes P2132/P2133, range P2131), while most current pedals carry only D and E, so the code can only occur on three-track pedals.
c: Pedal does not return fully to its stop
Poor contact at the pedal connector

P2118.d: P2118 looks at how much current throttle motor A needs. A healthy throttle moves with modest current; a high or abnormal draw means the motor is fighting resistance.
s: Limp-home mode after a cold start
No start or poor idle in frost
c: Ice on the throttle plate after a cold soak
Carbon or sludge loading the motor
Worn throttle motor or gear train
ECM logic too sensitive (software update available)

P2119.d: This is a mechanical performance check of the electronic throttle body. GM calls it Throttle Closed Position Performance: after the motor is de-energized the return springs must bring the plate into its default (limp) position, e.g.
c: Carbon deposits make the throttle plate stick
Water or ice in the intake behind the throttle body
Weak return spring or worn gear in the throttle body
ECM software that sets the code falsely (update available)

P211A.d: P211A means the second throttle on a twin-throttle engine stays further open than requested. Ford documents it in its 2020-2023 and 2024 summaries for applications with an ETB B, with MIL and wrench lamp and detection within 5 seconds; in 2024 it is shown as P210A with failure-type byte 72, matching P2111/P2100-72 for throttle A.
c: Ice or carbon holding throttle B open
Broken return spring or gear in throttle body B
Faulty throttle motor B or its position sensor

P211B.d: P211B is set when throttle B on a twin-throttle engine opens less than the controller asks for. Ford lists it for its dual-throttle applications in the 2020-2023 summary and in 2024 as P210A with failure-type byte 73, each with MIL, wrench lamp and detection in under 5 seconds; the A-side logic it mirrors is P2112, where actual angle trailing the target by more than 6 degrees counts as a fault.
c: Jammed gear or weak motor in throttle body B

P211C.d: P211C evaluates the current drawn by the second throttle motor. If throttle B needs clearly more current than expected to reach or hold its position, something is loading it mechanically or the motor itself is degrading.
c: Ice or condensate binding throttle B
Worn motor or gears in throttle body B

P211D.d: P211D is the mechanical check of throttle body B, the twin of P2119. GM's 23OBDG07 table describes four spring tests for bank 2: the opening and closing springs must bring the de-energized plate back to the defined limp position within set times (about 0.2-0.36 s per path), checked during offset learning and also at cold temperatures, each failing in one trip.
c: Weak or broken return spring in throttle body B
Deposits or ice slowing the plate
Throttle adaptation not completed after service

P211E.d: P211E is the processor fault for the control of throttle B on engines with two electronic throttles. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
s: Engine and ETC warning lamps on
c: Voltage dips or poor ground at the control unit
Internal hardware failure of the control unit

P211F.d: P211F covers a performance fault of the control function for throttle B, as distinct from a processor fault (P211E). No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
c: Throttle B responds or closes too slowly
Control unit software needing an update
Supply or ground problem at the control unit

P2120.d: P2120 is the general circuit check for signal D, which GM, Ford and VW all use for the first accelerator pedal track. GM's 2007 tables call it APP Sensor 1 Circuit: the ECM watches sensor 1 for steady or intermittent opens and shorts within its 0.325-4.75 V window and counts failures every 12.5 ms, setting the code at 19 of 39 counts.
s: Engine warning lamp and reduced power message
Fault often intermittent and hard to reproduce
c: Poor terminal tension or corrosion at pedal, inline or ECM connectors
Open or short in the sensor 1 signal, reference or ground wire
Internal fault in the pedal sensor, such as a cracked solder joint

P2121.d: P2121 means pedal signal D is electrically intact but implausible. Ford's 2012 OBD summary sets it only on second-generation ETC systems, whose pedals carry three tracks D, E and F: if sensor D disagrees with the others by more than 1.1 degrees, the PCM stores P2121 without MIL but with the wrench lamp, and pedal response becomes rate-limited using the healthy tracks.
s: Wrench or engine warning lamp on
Idle may rise when the brake is not pressed
c: Worn or dirty track D giving an offset reading
Contact resistance at the pedal connector
Shared reference or ground line shifting one signal

P2122.d: P2122 sets when pedal track D falls below its lower voltage limit, typically from a short to ground, a missing 5 V reference or a broken signal wire. Limits differ by maker: Ford uses 0.25 V and since 2020 lights both MIL and wrench lamp (in 2012 only the wrench lamp); GM's 2007 tables use 0.325 V with 19 of 39 counts at 12.5 ms (Type A), GM's 2023 table 23OBDG07 0.28 V for 0.2 s; the 2014 VW Passat flags anything un
s: Engine warning lamp and reduced power message
Pedal feels dead or reacts only slowly
c: Track D signal wire shorted to ground or chafed
Open or shorted 5 V reference feed to the pedal
Pedal sensor fault such as a cracked solder joint

P2123.d: P2123 is the high-voltage fault on pedal track D, usually an open sensor ground or a short to the 5 V reference or to battery voltage. GM's 2007 tables set it above 4.75 V (19 of 39 counts, Type A), a Bosch-based GM ECM from 2012 above 4.824 V lasting 0.2 s, and the 2014 VW Touareg above 4.89 V; Ford uses 4.75 V.
s: Engine warning lamp and reduced power message
Limited throttle opening despite full pedal
Fault may appear and vanish with harness movement
c: Open or high-resistance ground return of the pedal sensor
Track D signal shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage
Loose or spread terminals at pedal or inline connector

P2124.d: P2124 covers brief dropouts or spikes on pedal track D that come and go too quickly to count as a steady low or high fault. Ford documents it: special service messages 46829 (2015-2017 F-150) and 46880 (2017 Super Duty built up to late August 2017) tie P2124, alongside other pedal codes and wrench, ABS, airbag and hill descent lamps, to a pedal harness routed behind the bracket between brake booster and brake pedal,
s: Warning lamps that come and go, sometimes several at once
Brief loss of pedal response while driving
Reduced power mode after repeated dropouts
c: Pedal harness pinched or chafed by a misrouted path
Loose terminal or weak pin tension at the pedal connector
Worn spot on track D inside the pedal sensor

P2125.d: P2125 reports a general electrical fault in signal circuit E. GM uses it as Accelerator Pedal Position Sensor 2 Circuit: the ECM looks for a continuous or intermittent open or short in the sensor 2 circuit with a counter at 12.5 ms per count (19 of 39 counts).
s: Engine warning lamp and reduced power message
Traction control may be switched off
c: Internal fault in the pedal sensor (e.g. cracked solder joint)
Open or short in the sensor 2 wiring or 5 V reference
Loose or corroded pedal or inline connector

P2126.d: Signal E is electrically intact but its value does not fit the situation. Ford's 2012 OBD summary uses P2126 for the second pedal sensor on Gen2 throttle systems: it sets when sensors D and E disagree by more than 1.1 degrees, as a non-MIL fault with the wrench lamp.
s: Wrench or engine warning lamp on
Idle may be raised when braking
c: Worn or dirty sensor track E giving offset readings
Contact resistance at the pedal connector
Shared reference or ground circuit shifting one signal

P2127.d: P2127 reports that pedal track E reads below its lower limit. Because many pedals run the second track at roughly half the voltage of the first, the limit for E can sit lower than for D: GM's 2006 tables flag sensor 2 under 0.1625 V and the 2014 VW Passat under 0.27 V, against 0.61 V for track D.
s: Engine warning lamp, on newer Fords together with the wrench lamp
Reduced power and slower pedal response
Traction control may be switched off
c: Track E signal wire shorted to ground
Open 5 V reference feed for the second track
Worn track E at the closed-pedal end

P2128.d: P2128 sets when pedal track E reads above its upper limit, typically from an open sensor ground, a short to 5 V or a broken track. Where E is a half-scale signal the limit lies far below the supply: GM's 2006 tables flag sensor 2 above 2.295 V and the 2014 VW Passat above 2.43 V.
s: Engine warning lamp and reduced power message
Weak acceleration even with the pedal fully pressed
Often stored together with P2123 if the ground is open
c: Open or high-resistance ground of the pedal sensor
Track E signal shorted to the 5 V reference
Broken track or solder joint inside the pedal sensor

P2129.d: P2129 is meant for short dropouts or spikes in signal circuit E that do not last long enough for a steady low or high fault. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
s: Warning lamp that comes and goes
Brief hesitation or power loss while driving
Reduced power mode after repeated dropouts
c: Loose terminal or poor pin tension at the pedal connector
Worn spot or cracked joint inside the pedal sensor

P212A.d: P212A is the general circuit code for throttle position signal G, a letter that only comes into play on engines with more than one electronic throttle or extra position tracks. No manufacturer documents P212A publicly.
c: Open or short in the sensor G signal, supply or ground wire
Corroded or loose connector at the throttle body
Failed position sensor inside the throttle body

P212B.d: P212B means throttle signal G is electrically valid but its value does not fit. GM's 2023 table 23OBDG07 applies it to sensor 2 of the bank 2 throttle body on a twin-throttle engine: the code sets when the angle derived from sensor 2 differs from that of sensor 1 by more than about 5-6.25 %, or from the angle modelled from manifold pressure by more than 9 %, in one trip; the 2024 table repeats the check.
s: MIL on, often without noticeable driving problems
Reduced power if the plausibility fault persists
c: ECM software setting the code without a real fault (update available)
Sensor G drifted or worn, disagreeing with its partner sensor
Deposits or sticking plate making the angle disagree with airflow
Contact resistance at the throttle body connector

P212C.d: P212C sets when position signal G reads below its lower electrical limit. The letter G only comes into play on engines with more than one electronic throttle.
s: Uneven idle or hesitation on one bank
c: Signal wire of sensor G shorted to ground
5 V reference to the bank 2 throttle body open or pulled low
Worn or damaged track of position sensor G inside the throttle body
Corroded or loose terminals at the bank 2 throttle connector

P212D.d: P212D is the high-voltage fault on throttle position signal G. GM documents it in the 2023 and 2024 tables (23OBDG07, 24OBDG07) for sensor 2 of the bank 2 throttle body on a twin-throttle engine: once the raw voltage climbs above 4.805 V for 0.14 s, the code is stored in a single trip.
s: Weak or delayed response to the accelerator
c: Open sensor ground at the bank 2 throttle body
Signal wire of sensor G shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
Broken signal wire or pushed-back terminal
Internal fault in the position sensor of the bank 2 throttle

P212E.d: P212E is reserved for brief dropouts or spikes on throttle position signal G, the kind that clear again before a steady low or high fault can be confirmed. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
s: Warning lamp that comes and goes
Fault often not present at the workshop
c: Loose or worn terminal at the bank 2 throttle connector
Harness chafed by engine movement, breaking contact now and then
Moisture or corrosion in the connector
Momentary contact loss on the sensor track

P212F.d: P212F checks whether the two redundant signals F and G still agree in voltage. No manufacturer documents this code publicly, and the letters make it an unusual pair: GM's 2004-2005 truck tables use F for the third accelerator pedal track, while GM's 2023 table assigns G to the second sensor of a bank 2 throttle body.
s: Engine or throttle warning lamp on
c: One sensor track worn or drifted so the pair disagrees
Contact resistance in the connector shifting one signal
Fault in a shared ground or 5 V reference line

P2130.d: P2130 is the general circuit code for signal F. GM used it on its 2004-2005 pickups and SUVs with a separate throttle actuator control module (TACM) and a pedal carrying three tracks, where F is APP sensor 3.
s: Softer or delayed response to the pedal
Reduced power message on some models
c: Poor terminal contact or corrosion at the pedal connector
Open or short in the signal, reference or ground wire of track F
Third track inside the pedal sensor worn or failed
Faulty input in the throttle actuator control module or ECM

P2131.d: P2131 means pedal track F is electrically intact but disagrees with the rest of the pedal. Two makers document it for three-track pedals.
s: Wrench or engine warning lamp on
Often no noticeable change while driving
c: Worn or dirty track F giving an offset reading
Contact resistance at the pedal connector
Bent pedal bracket or binding mechanism distorting one track

P2132.d: P2132 sets when signal F drops below its lower voltage limit. Ford uses it for the third accelerator pedal track of its second-generation electronic throttle: its 2012 OBD summary treats anything under 0.25 V as a continuity fault and lights only the wrench lamp, not the MIL.
s: Wrench or engine warning lamp on
Idle may stay raised until the brake is pressed
c: Signal wire of track F shorted to ground
Open or weak 5 V reference to the pedal sensor
Track F worn at the rest position

P2133.d: P2133 is the high-voltage fault on signal F. In Ford's second-generation electronic throttle the third pedal track counts as failed once it rises above 4.75 V; the 2012 summary reports it with the wrench lamp and without MIL.
s: Wrench or engine warning lamp on
May appear together with high faults on other tracks if the ground is open
c: Open ground line of the pedal sensor
Signal wire of track F shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
Internal break in track F of the pedal sensor

P2134.d: P2134 targets short interruptions on signal F that are too brief or too irregular for a confirmed low or high fault. No manufacturer publishes a detection rule for it.
s: Warning lamp that appears and clears
Short hesitation when moving the pedal
c: Loose or spread terminal at the pedal connector
Pedal harness pinched or chafed near the footwell bracket
Worn spot on track F causing momentary contact loss

P2135.d: P2135 compares the two position tracks of the electronic throttle, A and B, and sets when they no longer describe the same plate angle. GM's 2006-2007 tables allow a 7 % offset at closed throttle rising to 10 % at full opening and count failures every 12.5 ms until 19 of 39 have failed.
s: Engine warning lamp or wrench lamp on
Reduced engine power, limited throttle opening
c: Worn or contaminated position tracks in the throttle body
Raised contact resistance or corrosion at the throttle connector
ECM calibration prone to false detection (update available on some models)
Fault on the shared 5 V reference or ground of both tracks

P2136.d: P2136 reports that position signals A and C disagree. On engines with two electronic throttles, C typically belongs to the second throttle body: GM's 2023 table 23OBDG07 assigns C to sensor 1 of the bank 2 throttle.
c: Increased resistance in the throttle actuator connector pins
Position sensor in one throttle body drifted or worn
Carbon or ice making one throttle lag behind the other

P2137.d: P2137 compares position signals B and C and sets when their voltages drift apart beyond the calibrated tolerance. No manufacturer publishes a detection rule for this pair; FCA merely lists P2137 in emissions recall T21 for the 2004-2006 Dodge Sprinter among the codes that may surface after the ECU is reprogrammed.
c: High resistance or corrosion at a throttle connector
Track B or sensor C drifted or worn
Fault on a shared 5 V reference or ground

P2138.d: P2138 is the standard plausibility check of a two-track accelerator pedal: D and E are pedal sensors 1 and 2 at GM, Ford and VW. GM's 2007 tables set it when the tracks differ by more than 10 % or their learned rest values by over 5 % (Type A); the 2023 table uses 0.12-0.18 V for 0.25 s in one trip.
s: Engine warning lamp with reduced engine power message
Traction or stability control may be switched off on some models
c: Water or corrosion in a pedal or inline harness connector
Worn pedal sensor with one track drifting
Poorly crimped or loose terminals raising resistance
Aftermarket equipment tapped into pedal or 5 V reference circuits

P2139.d: P2139 compares signals D and F, in practice the first and third tracks of a three-track accelerator pedal. No manufacturer publishes a detection rule for this exact code; FCA only lists P2139 in emissions recall T21 for the 2004-2006 Dodge Sprinter among codes that can appear after the ECU update.
s: Engine or wrench warning lamp on
c: Track D or F of the pedal sensor worn or drifted
Contact resistance at the pedal connector
Fault on a shared ground or 5 V reference

P213A.d: P213A concerns the electrical drive of EGR throttle B, a second motor-driven regulating flap found on some diesel layouts. Such a flap closes partly so that pressure ahead of the intake falls below exhaust pressure and enough exhaust gas can be recirculated; it also cuts air at engine stop.
c: Loose, corroded or broken connector or wire at throttle B
Open winding in the throttle B actuator motor
Harness damaged by heat near the exhaust or EGR cooler
Faulty output stage in the engine control module

P213B.d: P213B is the functional check of EGR throttle B rather than an electrical one. The module compares the position it commands with the position the flap actually reaches, or judges whether the feedback is plausible; if the gap persists beyond a set time, P213B is logged.
s: Hesitation, black smoke or reduced power
Clicking or humming from the flap
c: Flap stiff or stuck from soot and oil deposits
Worn gear train or weak actuator motor
Implausible position feedback from the flap sensor
Outdated engine software or missing flap adaptation

P213C.d: P213C points to a low signal in the drive circuit of EGR throttle B: the output stage sees too little voltage where it expects supply potential, which almost always means a conductor of the flap motor is touching ground. Chafed harness sections near the exhaust, water in the connector or a motor winding shorted to its housing are typical.
c: Chafed wire shorting to ground between module and flap
Water or corrosion in the flap connector
Actuator motor winding shorted to housing
Faulty output stage in the engine control module

P213D.d: P213D is the opposite electrical fault to P213C on EGR throttle B: the drive line carries voltage where the output stage expects ground, or the driver measures excessive current. A wire touching battery positive, a shorted motor winding that pulls too much current, or a mechanically blocked flap that overloads the motor are the usual triggers.
s: Reduced power in some operating ranges
c: Drive wire shorted to battery voltage
Shorted turns in the actuator motor causing overcurrent
Faulty output stage in the engine control module

P213E.d: P213E records that the engine module stopped the engine on purpose because of a fault on the injection side – rail, high-pressure lines, pressure control or injectors. Continuing to run with an external leak, a rail pressure that can no longer be controlled or an injector that keeps delivering could cause a fire or engine damage.
s: Engine cranks but does not start again
Fuel smell or visible fuel leak
Check engine lamp with further fuel system codes
c: External leak at rail, high-pressure line or injector seal
Injector stuck open or leaking heavily
Rail pressure control valve or sensor no longer controlling pressure
Engine software misjudging the fault, update available

P213F.d: P213F is the supply-side twin of P213E: the engine module shut the engine down because the fuel pump system – electric lift pump, its relay or control module, or the engine-driven high-pressure pump – no longer behaves in a way it can accept. No manufacturer documents P213F publicly, so the trigger is not known in detail.
s: No restart or very long cranking
Check engine lamp with fuel pump codes
c: Electric lift pump or its control module failed
Pump relay, fuse or wiring fault
Clogged filter or empty tank starving the pump

P2140.d: P2140 checks the second and third pedal tracks, E and F, against each other. As with P2139, no manufacturer explains its own trigger for this code, and FCA's emissions recall T21 for the 2004-2006 Dodge Sprinter just includes it in the list of codes that may follow the ECU reflash.
s: Engine or wrench warning lamp on
c: Track E or F of the pedal sensor worn or drifted
Shared 5 V reference or ground fault shifting one track
Contact resistance or moisture at the pedal connector

P2141.d: P2141 flags a low signal in the drive circuit of EGR throttle A, the main diesel regulating flap that lowers intake pressure so exhaust gas can flow back. A wire of the flap motor touching ground, a winding shorted to the housing or a wet connector are the common reasons.
c: Chafed wire shorting to ground between module and flap
Moisture or corrosion in the flap connector
Actuator motor winding shorted to housing
Faulty output stage in the engine control module

P2142.d: P2142 reports a high signal or overcurrent in the drive circuit of EGR throttle A. Either a motor lead has contact with battery voltage, or the motor draws more current than the output stage allows – from shorted turns or because carbon has jammed the blade.
c: Drive wire shorted to battery voltage
Flap jammed by carbon, motor overloaded
Shorted turns in the actuator motor
Faulty output stage in the engine control module

P2143.d: Vacuum-operated EGR valves are often run by a pair of solenoids: one feeds vacuum to the valve diaphragm to open it, the other – the vent solenoid – lets air in to release the vacuum and close the valve. Ford's EEC engine computers had separate outputs for EGR vent and EGR control, and a Kia diesel patent maps both solenoids by duty cycle, using the vent side whenever the measured EGR value is above target.
s: Rough idle or stalling after deceleration
c: Loose connector or broken wire at the vent solenoid
Open coil in the vent solenoid
Blown fuse or missing supply voltage to the solenoid
Faulty output stage in the engine control module

P2144.d: P2144 reports a low signal in the circuit that drives the EGR vent solenoid – the valve that bleeds vacuum from a vacuum-operated EGR valve so it can close. With the usual low-side switching, a control wire touching ground keeps the solenoid energised regardless of the command.
s: Emissions test failure because of EGR
c: Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Internal short in the vent solenoid coil
Corrosion bridging terminals in the connector
Faulty output stage in the engine control module

P2145.d: P2145 is the high fault in the vent solenoid circuit of the EGR system: the control line shows supply voltage while the module tries to pull it to ground, or the driver detects overcurrent through a shorted coil. The output then cannot switch the solenoid on, so the vent stays in its rest state – depending on design the EGR valve either cannot be released quickly or cannot be held, and the module normally stops using
s: EGR inactive, sometimes pinging under load on petrol engines
c: Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Shorted vent solenoid coil drawing excess current
Faulty output stage in the engine control module

P2146.d: Direct-injection and common-rail injectors are fed by a high-side driver in the engine module, often shared by several injectors. P2146 is the open or general fault of the first such supply.
s: Misfire on one or more cylinders
Rough running and loss of power
c: Injector harness chafed through or wire open inside insulation
Loose, wet or corroded injector connector
Open coil or piezo stack in an injector of the group
Faulty high-side driver in the engine control module

P2147.d: P2147 means the common feed of injector group A is pulled toward ground. GM documents it in detail for its 2018 Duramax diesels: the high-side line to injectors 1 and 4 (group 1 on both the 2.8 L four and the 6.6 L V8) shows 0.5 Ω or less to ground while the driver is switched on; with the engine running and more than 11 V, 5 failures in 10 samples at 100 ms set it, type A, lamp on the first trip (2025 tables: 4 of 8
s: Heavy loss of power, rough running
c: Injector supply wire chafed and shorted to ground
Injector of the group shorted internally to its body
Water in the injector harness connector
Faulty injector driver in the engine control module

P2148.d: P2148 flags group A's injector supply as too high. On GM's 2018 Duramax the high-side terminal of injector 1 or 4 shows 0.5 Ω or less to supply potential while the driver is off; same 5-of-10 counting at 100 ms, type A.
s: Misfire and rough running on the affected cylinders
Often no drivability complaint when the cause is software
c: Injector supply wire shorted to battery voltage
Internal fault of the injector boost circuit in the module
Software falsely detecting the fault, reprogramming available
Injector of the group with internal short

P2149.d: P2149 is the open or general fault of the second shared injector supply. Group membership depends on the engine: GM's 2009 Duramax places injectors 7 and 6 in group 2 (6 ms, type A), whereas GM's 2018 tables pair injectors 2 and 5 in the V8 – so the cylinders must be looked up for each engine.
s: Misfire on the cylinders of group B
c: Injector harness damaged or wire open
Water entering an injector harness connector
Open coil or piezo stack in an injector of the group
Low rail pressure from fuel vapour triggering follow-up faults

P214A.d: P214A reports that the exhaust entering the SCR catalyst was hotter than a calibrated ceiling while no particulate filter regeneration was active. The reading normally comes from the temperature sensor between the filter and the urea mixing section.
s: Reduced engine power to limit exhaust temperature
Further codes for exhaust temperature or SCR efficiency
c: Unburnt fuel or engine oil reaching the exhaust (leaking injector, turbocharger seal)
SCR inlet temperature sensor reading too high or wrongly placed after repair
Overfuelling from injection or air-path faults (boost leak, EGR fault)
Engine control software with outdated temperature model

P214B.d: P214B is limited to the regeneration phase. To burn soot out of the particulate filter, the engine control adds late injections or uses a separate exhaust fuel injector, and the oxidation catalyst converts that fuel into heat.
s: Check engine light on, regeneration aborted
Filter warning or rising soot load because regeneration cannot finish
c: Exhaust fuel injector leaking or over-dosing during regeneration
Heavily loaded filter burning off too quickly
Excess post-injection quantity from a worn engine injector
Exhaust temperature sensor upstream of the SCR reading too high

P214C.d: P214C looks at the downstream end of the SCR catalyst: the temperature measured behind it rose above the permitted maximum outside regeneration. California's OBD rule lists SCR intake and outlet temperature as separate data values a diesel must report, so both points are watched on their own.
s: Implausible outlet temperature compared with the inlet value in live data
c: SCR outlet temperature sensor faulty or reading too high
Hydrocarbons passing the oxidation catalyst and burning on the SCR
Fuel or oil entering the exhaust from the engine or turbocharger

P214D.d: P214D sets when the temperature behind the SCR catalyst exceeds its limit while the particulate filter is regenerating. It is the only code of this group with public manufacturer evidence.
c: Exhaust temperature sensor behind the SCR faulty, confused with another sensor or affected by low battery voltage
PCM software requiring an update (Ram 6.7L bulletins)
Regeneration fuel slipping through and burning on the SCR

P214E.d: P214E means the electronics driving the DEF (AdBlue) pump motor saw more current than the pump may draw. GM documents it on Duramax diesels: in the 2018 tables the DEF control module reports a motor high-current or current-limit error, and the ECM sets the code after 20 failed of 25 samples with the battery above 11 V; the 2025 tables use a hardware protection limit of 15 A plus separate motor current limits for pump
s: Check engine light on after one trip
DEF system warning, possibly a countdown to speed limitation
Raised NOx emissions because dosing stops
c: Pump motor seized, worn or blocked by crystallised or frozen fluid
Short in the pump motor winding or supply wiring, often after water ingress
ECM or reductant control module software (GM 20-NA-039)
Faulty driver stage in the reductant control module

P214F.d: P214F concerns heater A of the DEF system, which Ford and GM both assign to the heater inside the tank (heater circuit 1). The code says this element consumed more current or power than intended.
s: DEF system warning in cold weather
Delayed DEF dosing after cold starts
c: Tank heater element internally shorted (often replaced with the tank sender unit)
Water ingress or corrosion in the heater connector
Chafed heater wiring shorted to ground
Faulty heater driver in the reductant control module

P2150.d: P2150 reports the common feed of injector group B shorted toward ground. In GM's 2018 Duramax tables group 2 holds injectors 2 and 3 on the 2.8 L four-cylinder but injectors 2 and 5 on the 6.6 L V8; the test is the same as for group A – 0.5 Ω or less to ground with the driver on, 5 failed samples out of 10, type A with lamp on the first trip.
c: Group B supply wire chafed and shorted to ground
Injector of group B shorted to its body
Moisture in the injector harness connector
Faulty injector driver in the engine control module

P2151.d: P2151 marks the group B injector supply as too high. GM's 2018 Duramax checks the high-side pins of the bank 2 injectors with the driver switched off and sets the code at 0.5 Ω or less to supply potential, 5 of 10 samples, type A.
s: Misfire on the group B cylinders
Sometimes no noticeable symptom besides the lamp
c: Internal fault of the injector boost circuit in the module
Software falsely detecting the fault, reprogramming available
Group B supply wire shorted to battery voltage
Injector of group B with internal short

P2152.d: P2152 belongs to the third shared injector supply, so it appears only on engines with at least three injector groups or, at GM petrol engines, at least three cylinders. GM's 2009 Duramax puts injectors 2 and 5 into group 3 and flags an open, short or missing load after 6 ms, type A.
s: Misfire on the group C cylinders
c: Injector harness rubbed through at plenum, bolts or fuel line
Open coil or piezo stack in an injector of the group
Faulty power stage in the engine control module

P2153.d: P2153 reports the third shared injector supply shorted toward ground. GM's 2018 Duramax tables use it only for the 6.6 L V8, where bank 3 feeds injectors 6 and 7; the four-cylinder 2.8 L has just two banks and never sets it.
s: Misfire on the group C cylinders
c: Group C supply wire chafed and shorted to ground
Injector of group C shorted to its body
Moisture in the injector harness connector
Faulty injector driver in the engine control module

P2154.d: P2154 is the high fault of injector supply group C. On GM's 2018 Duramax V8 it covers injectors 6 and 7: with the driver off, 0.5 Ω or less from a high-side pin to supply potential in 5 of 10 samples sets it, type A, one trip.
s: Misfire on the group C cylinders
c: Internal hardware fault of the injector driver in the module
Group C supply wire shorted to battery voltage
Injector of group C with internal short

P2155.d: P2155 is the open or general fault of the fourth shared injector supply. On GM's 2009 Duramax V8 group 4 joins injectors 8 and 3; an open, short or missing load for 6 ms sets the code, type A.
s: Misfire on the group D cylinders
c: Injector harness damaged or wire open
Water entering an injector harness connector
Open coil or piezo stack in an injector of the group
Faulty power stage in the engine control module

P2156.d: P2156 reports the fourth shared injector supply shorted toward ground. GM's 2018 Duramax uses it only on the 6.6 L V8, where bank 4 combines injectors 3 and 8; the high-side pin reading 0.5 Ω or less to ground while switched on sets it after 5 of 10 samples, type A, lamp on the first trip.
c: Group D supply wire chafed and shorted to ground
Injector of group D shorted to its body
Moisture in the injector harness connector
Faulty injector driver in the engine control module

P2157.d: P2157 flags the group D injector supply as too high. GM's 2018 Duramax V8 tests the high-side pins of injectors 3 and 8 with the driver off; 0.5 Ω or less to supply potential in 5 of 10 samples sets it, type A, one trip, and the 2025 tables require 4 of 8.
s: Misfire on the group D cylinders
Several injector high codes stored together
c: Internal hardware fault of the injector driver in the module
Group D supply wire shorted to battery voltage
Injector of group D with internal short

P2158.d: P2158 reports an electrical fault in the circuit of a second vehicle speed signal, sensor B. P0500 is the matching code for sensor A.
s: Cruise control or ABS/traction functions unavailable
c: Speed sensor B defective or its tone ring damaged
Broken wire, corroded or loose connector in the sensor circuit
Retrofitted accessory interfering with the speed signal (Ducati anti-theft kit)

P2159.d: P2159 means the circuit of speed sensor B is electrically intact, but its signal does not fit: implausible jumps, dropouts or a value that disagrees with other speed sources. Two makers document it.
s: Check engine light or gearbox warning on
Erratic shifting or emergency gearbox mode
c: Faulty speed sensor or transmission sensor module (Audi 0B5)
Damaged tone ring, wrong air gap or metal debris on the sensor tip
Intermittent contact in wiring or connector
Wrong tyre size or speed factor configured

P215A.d: P215A compares the vehicle speed used by the powertrain with the speed derived from the ABS wheel sensors and sets when the two disagree. Volvo and Mack trucks document it most clearly: with I-Shift or mDRIVE gearboxes the code appears once the difference exceeds 12 km/h (7.5 mph), and the advice is to verify the speed factor and the tyre size stored in the brake controller before testing sensors.
s: ABS, traction or cruise control warnings, power dropouts
c: Tyre size or speed factor not matching the vehicle (common after tyre or axle changes)
Faulty wheel speed sensor or damaged tone ring
Poor ABS module ground or wiring fault in the speed signal path
Fault in the transmission-side vehicle speed source

P215B.d: P215B checks whether the vehicle speed, as the control unit has chosen it, matches the speed implied by the transmission output shaft. GM uses it widely in hybrids and EVs.
s: Check engine light on after one trip
ABS, traction or stability lamps, systems switched off for the drive
Clicking noise from a front wheel (Bolt EV)
c: Damaged wheel speed sensor (GM Bolt EV broken anti-click washer)
Faulty transmission output speed sensor or its wiring
Hybrid or transmission control software (FCA Pacifica Hybrid)
Lost speed message from another module on the data bus

P215C.d: P215C compares the transmission output shaft speed with the output speed calculated back from the wheel sensors. Unlike P215B it does not judge the final vehicle speed but the agreement between these two measured sources.
s: Grinding noise or loss of all-wheel drive (transfer unit damage)
c: Transmission control software too sensitive, for example under braking (FCA bulletins)
Mechanical driveline fault such as a broken transfer unit spline (Jeep Cherokee)
Faulty output shaft speed sensor or wiring
Faulty wheel speed sensor or mismatched tyre sizes

P215D.d: P215D says the second DEF pump, called pump B or pump 2, keeps running or stays powered although the controller has commanded it off. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
s: Pump audible after switching off the engine
DEF system warning, possibly a flat battery after standing
c: Output stage in the control module no longer switching off
Pump control line shorted so the pump receives power permanently
Welded contacts in the pump supply relay

P215E.d: P215E says the fourth DEF heating element, heater D, drew less current than expected while it was switched on, so it is probably not warming the fluid. Which element carries the letter D depends on the maker; many SCR systems stop at three.
s: Check engine light together with a DEF or emission system message
Dosing starts late or not at all after cold starts in frost
Restart countdown or speed limitation if the fault stays active
c: Heating element D open or burnt through, often inside a heated line or pump assembly
Corroded or loose pins at the heater D connector limiting current
Heater feed fuse or relay open, so the element gets no voltage
Weak heater output stage in the engine or DEF control module

P215F.d: P215F is set when heater D of the DEF system pulls more current than its design allows, which points to a partly shorted element or a leak path to ground in its wiring. The letter D is assigned by each maker, and many systems have only three heaters.
s: Check engine light with a DEF or emission system warning
DEF stays frozen in the affected area during cold weather
Blown heater fuse in some cases
c: Heating element D partly shorted internally
Moisture or DEF crystals in the heater D connector bridging pins
Chafed heater lead touching ground or a neighbouring circuit

P2160.d: P2160 reports that speed signal B shows little or no activity although the vehicle is plainly moving. Which pickup carries the letter B is the manufacturer's choice.
s: Check engine lamp after two drives
Speedometer or cruise control misbehaving on some models
c: Broken signal wire or short to ground between sensor B and the module
Speed sensor B itself delivers no pulses
Corroded or pushed-back pins at the sensor connector
Tone wheel loose or missing after transfer case or driveline work

P2161.d: P2161 flags a speed signal B that behaves in ways no real vehicle can: it collapses for a moment, jumps or reads implausibly high. GM documents the code for the transfer case output speed sensor (18OBDG04).
s: Check engine lamp, often only on rough roads
c: Connector contact opening briefly under vibration
Signal wire chafed against the transfer case or frame
Metal debris on the magnetic sensor tip

P2162.d: P2162 means two speed sources, A and B, disagree by more than the calibration permits although each circuit is electrically sound. Depending on the vehicle, A and B can be a transmission output sensor, a transfer case sensor or wheel sensors read through the ABS unit.
s: Harsh or mistimed shifts, possibly a fixed-gear fallback
c: Tyre size or axle ratio differs from the programmed values
Metal debris or damage on one of the two sensors
Damaged or wrong tone wheel on one shaft or hub
Wheel speed signal from the ABS unit faulty

P2163.d: P2163 concerns position signal A at the upper end of its travel: with the throttle or pedal resting on its maximum mechanical stop, the reading or the learned full-open value lies outside the band the calibration accepts. On Ford layouts A is the first throttle body sensor, while D to F belong to the pedal.
s: Check engine and throttle warning lamps on
Engine does not reach full power
Limp mode with limited throttle opening
c: Carbon or a bent stop keeps the plate from reaching full opening
Sensor A track worn at the full-open end
Replacement throttle body not matching or not relearned
Contact resistance in the sensor connector shifting the signal

P2164.d: P2164 is the full-travel test for position signal B. When the throttle or pedal is held at its upper stop, sensor B has to report a value inside a calibrated band; a reading or learned maximum outside that band sets the code.
s: Power limited at high throttle demand
c: Sensor B track worn or drifted at the full-open end
Deposits or a damaged stop limit the plate travel
Corroded contact on the sensor B signal or reference pin
End positions not relearned after part replacement

P2165.d: P2165 belongs to the rarely used letter C. It is set when position signal C, at the upper stop of its throttle or pedal, reports a value the controller cannot accept as full travel.
c: Sensor C track worn at the end of travel
Replacement throttle or pedal with a different characteristic
Mechanical obstruction before the upper stop
Resistance in the sensor C wiring or connector

P2166.d: P2166 refers to position signal D, which on Ford designs is the first track of the accelerator pedal. The code means the reading with the pedal pressed all the way does not match the calibrated maximum, for instance because the pedal never reaches its stop or the track is worn at the far end.
s: No kickdown or no full power with the pedal floored
c: Floor mat or object keeps the pedal from its stop
Pedal sensor track D worn at full travel
Bent pedal arm or damaged pedal bracket
Corroded pedal connector shifting signal D

P2167.d: P2167 checks position signal E at maximum travel; on designs that call the pedal tracks D, E and F, E is the second pedal sensor. The code sets when E, with the pedal fully down, reports a value outside the accepted band.
s: Limited power with the pedal fully pressed
c: Pedal sensor track E worn at the full-travel end
Contact corrosion in the pedal connector
Pedal cannot reach its stop (mat, object, bent bracket)

P2168.d: P2168 covers position signal F at maximum travel. Letter F only exists where the pedal carries a third sensor track; GM's 2004 engine table, for example, runs a third pedal sensor under the F circuit codes, whereas most current cars make do with two tracks.
c: Third pedal track F worn at full travel
Poor contact on the sensor F pins
Pedal held short of its stop

P2169.d: The name points to a solenoid that lets an exhaust pressure regulator vent, but the only public, code-exact use found is on Jaguar Land Rover petrol models, where this code family belongs to the active exhaust valve: a solenoid in the tailpipe section switches a flap between quiet and sport sound. P2169 is the open or general fault of its control line.
s: Exhaust sound no longer changes with the drive mode
c: Vehicle configuration enables an active exhaust valve that is not fitted
Broken wire or loose connector at the exhaust valve solenoid, often from heat or road dirt

P216A.d: Injector group E exists only on engines with at least five cylinders or five separately fed injector groups. GM petrol direct injection uses one group per cylinder, and its 2024 tables (24OBDG07) state it plainly: injector E is cylinder 5.
s: Check engine lamp on, often with a cylinder 5 misfire code
c: Injector harness rubbed through at the intake plenum, valve cover bolts or fuel line
High-side driver in the engine control module faulty

P216B.d: P216B reports the feed of injector group E pulled toward ground. In GM petrol direct injection, group E means the injector of cylinder 5, so the code appears on V6 and V8 engines.
c: High-side wire of injector 5 chafed through to ground, for example on the transmission
Cylinder 5 injector shorted to its housing
Engine control module output stage faulty

P216C.d: P216C is the opposite fault of group E: the feed of the cylinder 5 injector carries voltage when it should not. GM tests it while the high-side driver is switched off; if 1 V or less remains between the signal and the controller supply, the line is treated as shorted to power.
c: Injector 5 feed chafed against a powered circuit
High-side driver in the engine control module leaking voltage
Moisture or corrosion bridging pins in the injector connector

P216D.d: P216D is the general fault of injector group F, which GM petrol direct injection equates with cylinder 6; its 2024 tables (24OBDG07) call it injector F. GM uses this code for shorts on the high side rather than opens: the 2008 3.6 LLT sets it for cylinder 6 shorted to ground or battery, while an open on either side goes to P0206; the 2024 tables count two events of less than 0.5 ohm to ground or supply, above 9 V, on
s: Check engine lamp on, cylinder 6 misfire
With the LT6 several bank 2 codes and fuel pressure faults at once
c: Injector harness rubbed through on V6 engines
Water in the bank 2 injector harness connector (Corvette LT6)

P216E.d: P216E marks the feed of injector group F, the cylinder 6 injector on GM petrol direct injection, as shorted toward ground. It therefore concerns GM V6 and V8 engines with direct injection.
s: Cylinder 6 misfire and loss of power
c: Cylinder 6 feed wire chafed through to ground
Engine control module output stage faulty

P216F.d: P216F is set when the group F supply, on GM petrol direct injection the high-side line of cylinder 6, shows voltage while the driver is off. GM's criterion in its 2016 (16OBDG07A) and 2018 LT4 tables is 1 V or less between the line and the controller supply, which means the wire is practically at battery level.
c: Cylinder 6 feed shorted to another powered wire
Engine control module driver fault, especially with several high codes

P2170.d: P2170 reports the control line of the exhaust pressure regulator vent solenoid pulled toward ground. Jaguar Land Rover uses it for the solenoid of the active exhaust valve; its March 2018 shop foreman call lists P2170-11, meaning the line is grounded, on 2018 Discovery Sport and Evoque with active exhaust.
s: Restricted performance message on some models
Exhaust valve heard clicking at start-up
c: PCM software with an overly sensitive fault strategy, fixed by an update
Exhaust flap stiff, often from a misaligned heat shield or cold weather
Control wire chafed through to ground near the exhaust

P2171.d: P2171 means the module sees too much voltage on the control line of the exhaust pressure regulator vent solenoid, usually because the line touches battery voltage or the solenoid shorts internally. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly.
s: Exhaust flap stays in one position
c: Control wire shorted to a battery-fed circuit
Output stage in the engine control module faulty

P2172.d: P2172 is set when the engine abruptly takes in far more air than the throttle opening can explain, as if a large leak had appeared behind the throttle plate. The controller compares measured airflow (MAF or MAP based) with the flow its throttle model expects and reacts to a quick jump in the difference.
s: High or hunting idle, hissing noise from the engine bay
c: Hose, PCV line or brake booster line slipped off or split
Spread or pushed-out terminals at the MAP sensor connector
Engine software with oversensitive detection (reflash available)

P2173.d: P2173 reports an air surplus that builds up gradually: across a longer stretch of driving the engine receives more air than the throttle model predicts, which points to a small leak, a cracked vent hose or a plate that no longer seals. FCA calls it High Airflow/Vacuum Leak Detected (Slow Accumulation).
s: Check engine lamp after some driving
Start/stop system deactivated on some models
c: Cracked or loose crankcase ventilation or oil vapour tube
Small leak at an intake gasket or vacuum hose
MAP sensor connector with poor contact

P2174.d: P2174 means the airflow fell abruptly well below what the current throttle opening should deliver. The controller sees a fast negative gap between measured airflow and its throttle-model estimate, as happens when the intake is suddenly blocked, the plate jams or a hose collapses under vacuum.
s: Check engine and throttle warning lamps
c: Air inlet suddenly blocked by snow, leaves or debris
Throttle plate sticking short of the commanded angle
Airflow or manifold pressure sensor reading too low

P2175.d: P2175 tracks an air shortfall that develops slowly: over many operating points the engine receives less air than the throttle position predicts, and the learned correction finally exceeds its limit. A clogged air filter, carbon narrowing the throttle bore, a partly blocked intake or an airflow sensor drifting low are the usual reasons.
c: Carbon build-up narrowing the throttle bore
Heavily clogged air filter or intake restriction
Idle or airflow adaptation not reset after throttle cleaning

P2176.d: P2176 says the closed rest position of throttle A could not be learned. At key-on or after shutdown the controller drives the plate onto its lower stop and stores the sensor values; if they stay outside the window after the permitted attempts, the code is set.
s: Check engine lamp right after start
Reduced engine power after a cold start
c: Carbon on plate and bore preventing a clean closed position
Ice from a frozen crankcase ventilation holding the plate open
Engine software misjudging the sensor signals (update available)
Idle learn not performed after cleaning or module replacement

P2177.d: P2177 means bank 1's long-term trim has to add too much fuel once the engine is off idle, at part load and while accelerating. Bosch-type systems learn this as a multiplicative factor that scales with airflow, unlike the additive idle part behind P2187.
s: Check engine lamp on after two trips
Hesitation or lack of power when accelerating
c: Fuel pressure too low under load, for example a weak pump or clogged filter
Air mass sensor reading too low or contaminated
Leak after the air mass sensor, often on the boost side
Calibration error or damaged A/F sensor wiring covered by bulletins

P2178.d: P2178 is the rich-side limit of the bank 1 load adaptation: above idle the long-term trim has to take away more fuel than allowed. GM's Bosch-based V6 engines of 2005 and 2008 set it below a factor of 0.78, the 2023 and 2024 tables below 0.77, each after two trips.
s: Check engine lamp on after two trips
c: Air mass sensor reading too high
Fuel pressure too high or injectors over-delivering
Calibration error fixed by a software update
Fuel vapour from purge or boiling fuel in the low-pressure system

P2179.d: P2179 is the bank 2 version of P2177 on engines with a front oxygen sensor for each cylinder bank: the load-dependent, multiplicative share of bank 2's long-term correction has reached its lean limit. GM's 2005 2.8 and 3.6 V6 and the 2008 3.6 LLT use a factor above 1.23, GM's 2024 tables above 1.27, both over two trips.
s: Check engine lamp on after two trips
c: Low fuel pressure or air mass sensor fault, usually with P2177 too
Intake leak or front oxygen sensor fault on bank 2

P217A.d: Group G only exists on engines with seven or more injector groups, in practice eight-cylinder engines with direct injection. GM's 2023 and 2024 summary tables (23OBDG07, 24OBDG07) name the cylinder 7 injector G and use P217A for a short on its high side: less than 0.5 ohm between the module pin and ground while the driver is off, or to the injector supply while it is on.
s: Check engine lamp on, cylinder 7 misfire
c: Cylinder 7 injector feed shorted to ground or supply in the harness

P217B.d: P217B reports the feed of injector group G as grounded, which on GM's direct-injection V8 engines is the injector of cylinder 7, at the rear of bank 1. GM's 2016 table 16OBDG07A and the 2018 LT4 table of the supercharged 6.2 V8 measure it with the driver switched on: if 25 A or more flows through the high side, the line is grounded somewhere.
c: Cylinder 7 feed wire grounded at the rear of the engine
Engine control module output stage faulty

P217C.d: P217C means the group G injector supply, cylinder 7 on GM's direct-injection V8 engines, is pulled up to supply voltage. GM tests this while the high-side driver is off: if the line sits within 1 V of the controller supply, the module treats it as shorted to power.
c: Cylinder 7 feed shorted to a powered wire

P217D.d: Group H is the eighth injector group, on GM petrol direct injection the injector of cylinder 8, the last one on bank 2 of a V8. GM's 2023 and 2024 tables call it injector H and use P217D when its high side shows less than 0.5 ohm to ground with the driver off or to the injector supply with the driver on; two events above 9 V store the code in one trip.
s: Check engine lamp on, cylinder 8 misfire
Several bank 2 injector codes at once if the connector is wet
c: Water in the bank 2 injector harness connector, Corvette LT6
Cylinder 8 injector feed shorted in the harness

P217E.d: P217E flags the supply of injector group H as grounded, on GM's direct-injection V8 engines the injector of cylinder 8. GM lists it for the 6.2 LT4 in 2018 and in its 2016 table 16OBDG07A.
c: Cylinder 8 feed wire chafed to ground
Cylinder 8 injector shorted to its housing
Engine control module output stage faulty

P217F.d: P217F is the last code of the injector group series: the feed of group H, cylinder 8 on GM's direct-injection V8 engines, shows supply voltage although the high-side driver is switched off. GM's tables 16OBDG07A, 18OBDG03A for the 6.2 LT4 and 19OBDG03A set it when the line stays within 1 V of the controller supply, counting 10 failures out of 20 samples at 100 ms with 11 V or more, type A, MIL on the first trip.
s: Cylinder 8 misfire, possibly rich running on bank 2
c: Cylinder 8 feed shorted to a powered wire
Moisture or corrosion in the injector connector
Engine control module output stage faulty

P2180.d: P2180 closes the series: bank 2's long-term trim must remove too much fuel above idle, so its multiplicative adaptation sits at the rich limit. GM's 2005 2.8 and 3.6 V6 and the 2008 3.6 LLT use a factor below 0.78, GM's 2024 tables below 0.77, both over two trips.
s: Check engine lamp on after two trips
c: Injector on bank 2 leaking or over-delivering
Fuel pressure too high or air mass sensor over-reading, usually with P2178
Bank 2 front oxygen sensor reading rich

P2181.d: P2181 is the engine computer's verdict that the coolant warms up too slowly or settles below its target, almost always because the thermostat no longer closes. CARB requires the thermostat to be monitored and flags a failure when the warm-up stays more than 11.1 °C under the regulating point.
s: Check engine light, usually without any change in driving behaviour
Temperature gauge rises slowly or stays below normal
Weak cabin heating in cold weather
Higher fuel consumption on short trips
c: Thermostat not closing fully because of wear, corrosion or debris on the seat
Engine control software too sensitive, fixed by a reflash on some models (e.g. Kia SA463)
Radiator fan running constantly and overcooling the engine
Low coolant level or air in the system distorting the temperature reading

P2182.d: P2182 is the general circuit code for the second coolant temperature sensor: the module sees a fault in its wiring or signal but does not sort it into low, high or erratic. Where sensor 2 sits is up to the maker.
s: Radiator fan runs continuously as a precaution
c: Loose, corroded or water-damaged connector at sensor 2
Signal or reference wire to sensor 2 open or damaged

P2183.d: P2183 means sensor 2 delivers a voltage inside the valid band, yet the temperature does not fit the other readings. Most makers test this after a long cold soak, when all temperatures should match.
s: Check engine light, often right after a cold start
Remote start disabled on some trucks
Engine overheat message without real overheating on some hybrids
c: Water ingress or internal corrosion in sensor 2 shifting its reading
Control software misjudging soak time, block heater or cabin heater use
Coolant hoses at the sensor loop swapped or air trapped after service
Aged sensor element drifting out of tolerance

P2184.d: Coolant sensors are NTC thermistors: the hotter they get, the lower their resistance and voltage. P2184 therefore reports a signal from sensor 2 so low that it would mean an impossibly hot engine, typically a signal wire touching ground or a shorted sensor.
s: Check engine light after two drives on GM vehicles
Radiator fans running at full speed
Further codes and warnings if a harness is chafed
c: Signal wire of sensor 2 chafed through and touching ground
Coolant or water in the connector bridging signal and ground

P2185.d: P2185 is the high end of the sensor 2 circuit check. With an NTC thermistor a high signal stands for extreme cold, so the usual reason is an open circuit: a broken wire, an unplugged or corroded connector, or a sensor with an interrupted element; a short to voltage is rarer.
s: Fans run permanently as a safety measure
Low coolant or temperature warning without a real cause on some models
c: Connector at sensor 2 unplugged, loose or corroded
Signal or ground wire of sensor 2 broken
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source

P2186.d: P2186 covers a sensor 2 signal that jumps instead of changing smoothly. Coolant temperature moves slowly because of the mass of the liquid, so a step faster than physics allows points to a loose contact rather than a real change.
s: Check engine light after two drives
Fans switching on and off irregularly
Temperature-related messages that appear and vanish
c: Worn or loose pins in the sensor 2 connector
Wire broken inside its insulation or chafed harness making intermittent contact
Sensor 2 with an intermittent internal fault

P2187.d: P2187 means the long-term fuel trim of bank 1 has to add more fuel than allowed in the idle and low-load range. Many systems, especially Bosch ones, split mixture adaptation into an additive part, which dominates at low airflow, and a multiplicative part for load.
s: Rough or hunting idle, hissing from the engine bay
c: Air leak after the air mass sensor, often at the crankcase ventilation
Damaged front oxygen or A/F sensor wiring

P2188.d: P2188 means the long-term fuel trim of bank 1 has to remove more fuel than allowed in the idle and low-load range, the additive part of the mixture adaptation on Bosch-type systems. GM's 2008 3.6 LLT sets it below -6.0 % at 520 to 1120 rpm and 1.7 to 7.8 g/s, with closed loop and coolant above 60 °C.
c: Leaking injector or fuel pressure too high
Fuel vapour from the purge valve or oil-diluted crankcase gases
Air mass or manifold pressure reading wrong

P2189.d: P2189 is the bank 2 version of P2187: on engines with a front oxygen sensor per bank, the long-term trim of bank 2 has to add more fuel than allowed at idle and low load. GM's 2005 2.8 and 3.6 V6 set it when the additive correction exceeds 7 %, the 2008 3.6 LLT above 6.1 % at 520 to 1120 rpm, airflow of 1.7 to 7.8 g/s, engine load of 11 to 45 % and coolant above 60 °C, and GM's 2024 tables above about 5.5 % over two
c: Intake gasket or runner leak on the bank 2 side
Shared vacuum leak, usually with P2187 present too
Bank 2 front sensor, its wiring or an injector on that bank

P218A.d: P218A is the throttle B counterpart of P2176: on engines with a second electronic throttle, usually one per cylinder bank, that second unit failed to learn its closed rest position. GM's 2023 table 23OBDG07 runs the same three-step learn for bank 2 as for bank 1.
c: Carbon or ice keeping throttle B off its closed stop
Weak motor or gear wear in throttle unit B
Position sensors of throttle B outside the learn window
Supply or signal wiring fault at throttle B

P218B.d: P218B is a general electrical fault in the second throttle/fuel inhibit line, B. An inhibit line carries a signal with which another unit can tell the engine computer to keep the throttle closed or stop fuelling.
s: Check engine lamp on the following drive
c: Open or high-resistance inhibit B wire
Corroded or loose pins at the engine or throttle module connector
Fault in the unit that drives the inhibit signal

P218C.d: P218C means the inhibit B line is electrically within limits, yet its state or response does not fit what the controller expects: it may signal a lock when none is requested, or fail to react during a function test. No manufacturer documents P218C publicly.
s: Check engine lamp on the next drive
Occasional power reduction without obvious reason
c: Relay in the inhibit path sticking or switching late
Software versions of the communicating modules do not match
Intermittent contact causing implausible line states

P218D.d: P218D reports that the voltage on inhibit line B sits below the lowest permitted value, which normally points to a short to ground, a missing supply from the sending unit or an open line pulled down by the input stage. No manufacturer documents P218D publicly.
s: Check engine lamp on the following drive
c: Inhibit B wire shorted to ground
Water or corrosion in a connector of the inhibit line
Output stage of the sending module failed

P218E.d: P218E says the inhibit B line carries more voltage than the controller allows, typically because it touches a battery-fed wire or the sending unit's output stage is stuck high. No manufacturer documents P218E publicly.
s: Check engine lamp on the following drive
c: Inhibit B wire shorted to a battery-fed circuit
Voltage fed back through a faulty module after ignition off
Relay contacts welded, keeping the line energised

P218F.d: P218F means the SCR system is dosing on paper, but nothing reaches the exhaust: the expected link between dosing commands, pump effort and line pressure is missing. Ford's 2023 diesel summary, which calls the test a reductant delivery check for clogging, runs it while dosing with the pressure error inside 0.5 bar for 5 s.
s: Check engine light with a DEF or emission system warning
Restart countdown or speed limitation if the fault persists
White crystalline deposits at the dosing valve or line joints
c: Dosing valve or its nozzle crystallised and blocked
Leak in the DEF line between pump and dosing valve
Partly frozen line in frost or control software that needs an update
Worn DEF pump that cannot keep up delivery

P2190.d: P2190 is the bank 2 counterpart of P2188: the long-term trim of bank 2 has to remove more fuel than allowed at idle and low load. GM's 2008 3.6 LLT sets it below -6.0 % in the same window it uses for P2188 (520 to 1120 rpm, 1.7 to 7.8 g/s, closed loop, coolant above 60 °C, catalyst heating not active), and GM's 2005 2.8 and 3.6 V6 treat it in the same additive adaptation range.
c: Shared cause such as air mass error or purge vapour, usually with P2188 too

P2191.d: P2191 sets once bank 1's long-term trim has run into its enrichment limit in the upper load range, so the engine would be lean there without the correction. It is the third load zone next to P2187 (idle) and P2177 (off idle), and it is where a supply that copes at cruise first falls short: a tired fuel pump, a clogged filter, poor pressure regulation, injectors that flow too little, or an air mass sensor that reads l
s: Hesitation or flat spot under heavy throttle
Loss of power when climbing or towing
High positive long-term fuel trim at high load only
c: Fuel pump or pressure regulation unable to hold pressure at high demand
Air mass sensor under-reading at high airflow
Charge-air or intake leak behind the air mass sensor (turbo engines)

P2192.d: P2192 is the rich-side limit of the bank 1 trim in the upper load zone: the controller has pulled as much fuel as it may and the front sensor still reports excess fuel. Typical sources grow with demand, such as an air mass sensor reading high, fuel pressure above specification, or injectors that over-deliver or drip at high rail pressure; on direct-injection engines a leaking high-pressure injector is a prime suspect
s: Fuel smell or dark exhaust under load
c: ECM calibration issue covered by a software update (e.g. Kia 1.6 GDI)
Air mass sensor reading too high
Injector leaking or over-delivering at high rail pressure

P2193.d: P2193 reports for bank 2 what P2191 reports for bank 1: in the upper load zone the long-term trim of that bank sits at its enrichment limit. It only exists on engines with a separate front sensor per bank, such as V6, V8 and boxer engines.
s: Bank 2 long-term trim much higher than bank 1 at high load
c: Weak fuel supply (pump, filter, pressure regulation), usually with P2191
Intake gasket or runner leak on the bank 2 side
Exhaust leak ahead of the bank 2 front sensor

P2194.d: P2194 means bank 2 has reached the lower limit of its trim in the upper load zone: the ECM is removing as much fuel as permitted, yet that bank still runs rich. Because air mass, fuel pressure and canister purge feed both banks, a rich error caused by them usually brings P2192 along.
s: Bank 2 long-term trim strongly negative at high load
c: Leaking or over-delivering injector on bank 2
Air mass sensor reading high or fuel pressure too high (usually with P2192)

P2195.d: P2195 means the front oxygen or air-fuel sensor on bank 1 reports a lean mixture that the ECM does not believe, either because it stays lean or because it disagrees with other evidence. On GM's Bosch-based 2005 V6 the rear sensor has to read rich (above 0.85 V) while the front A/F sensor reads leaner than lambda 1.08 and the short-term trim sits at its maximum of 1.25, for about 100 s or 50 s in total.
s: Possible rough running or higher consumption from wrong fuelling
c: Front oxygen or A/F sensor aged or contaminated
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor
Sensor signal or reference wiring fault

P2196.d: P2196 means the front oxygen or air-fuel sensor on bank 1 reports a rich mixture that the ECM does not accept. On GM's Bosch-based 2005 V6 this is a cross-check with the rear sensor: the rear sensor reads lean (below 0.15 V) while the front A/F sensor reads richer than lambda 0.92 and the short-term trim has pulled to its minimum of 0.75, for about 100 s or 50 s in total.
c: Front oxygen or A/F sensor contaminated or aged
Sensor signal shorted or reference circuit fault

P2197.d: P2197 is the bank 2 version of P2195 on engines with a front sensor per bank: the bank 2 front oxygen or A/F sensor keeps reporting lean in a way the ECM rejects. GM's Bosch-based 2005 2.8 and 3.6 V6 flag it when the bank 2 rear sensor reads rich (above 0.85 V) while the front sensor reads leaner than lambda 1.08 with short-term trim at its 1.25 maximum, a contradiction a real lean mixture would not produce.
s: Possible rough running or higher consumption
c: Bank 2 front oxygen or A/F sensor aged or contaminated
Exhaust manifold leak on bank 2 ahead of the sensor

P2198.d: P2198 is the bank 2 counterpart of P2196: the bank 2 front oxygen or A/F sensor reports rich in a way the ECM does not accept. On GM's Bosch-based 2005 2.8 and 3.6 V6 the bank 2 rear sensor must read lean (below 0.15 V) while the front sensor reads richer than lambda 0.92 and the short-term trim has dropped to its 0.75 minimum; the code then sets after about 100 s, or 50 s cumulatively, over two trips.
c: Bank 2 front oxygen or A/F sensor contaminated or aged
Sensor signal or reference wiring fault
